title: Ingest email into your workspace
summary: Poll an email connection on a schedule and store each message as a durable, searchable email — the foundation every email automation builds on.
body_md:
# Ingest email into your workspace

Pull messages from a mailbox on a cadence and store each one as a durable email you
can search, label, and drive further automations from. Nothing is provisioned until
you build this automation — an email *connection* is just dormant credentials.

## 1. Register the connection (one-time)

`POST /email/connections` with a `provider` and its fields:

- `maildir` — `root`, `mailbox`
- `imap` — `host`, `port`, `username`, `password`, `mailbox`
- `jmap` — `session_url`, `token`, `account_id`
- `gmail` — `client_id`, `client_secret`, `refresh_token`, `label`

The response gives you a connection **id** (a uuid). Registering *provisions nothing* —
the connection stays dormant until a `collect_email` automation references it.
`GET /email/connections` reports `collecting: true` once one does.

## 2. Build the collect automation

The head node is the **`collect_email`** trigger — a *source/poll* trigger, not an
event matcher. Every `every` interval it drains new messages and fires one automation
run **per message, in order, inline**. Wire it to a **`write_email`** action, the only
node that actually persists mail: an idempotent upsert keyed by `(mailbox, uid)` that
then enqueues chunk → embed → project, so the message becomes semantically searchable.

```json
{ "graph": {
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "collect", "kind": "trigger", "trigger": {
        "kind": "collect_email",
        "connection": "<connection-id>",
        "mailbox": "INBOX",
        "every": "5m",
        "backfill_window": { "days": 7 },
        "commit_on": "store"
    }, "position": { "x": 0, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "store", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "write_email", "archive_raw": true
    }, "position": { "x": 260, "y": 0 } }
  ],
  "edges": [ { "from": "collect", "to": "store" } ]
}}
```

`POST /automations` with this spec (or author it in the visual editor / via the
`create_automation` tool).

## 3. Trigger config that matters

- **`connection`** (required) — the connection id to pull from.
- **`mailbox`** — narrow to one folder; omit for the connection default.
- **`filter`** — `{ "sender": "…", "subject": "…", "body": "…" }`; case-insensitive
  substrings, AND-ed together. Only matching messages are ingested.
- **`every`** — poll cadence: bare minutes (`5`), `{ "minutes": 5 }` /
  `{ "seconds": 30 }`, or a duration string (`"30s"`, `"5m"`, `"1h30m"`, `"1y"`). Clamped to
  `[60s, 1 year]`.
- **`backfill_window`** — how far back the *first* poll reaches: a bare number = days,
  or `{ "days" | "hours" | "minutes": N }`. Unset defaults to **1 day**.
- **`commit_on`** — the downstream node id whose success commits the message (below).

The twin **`collect_calendar`** trigger + **`write_event`** action ingest calendar
events the same way — swap `mailbox` for `calendar`.

## 4. How committing and the cursor work

Each connection keeps a per-source **ledger** packed into its `sync_token`: a cursor
plus the set of committed message uids, persisted after **every item**, so a crash
re-runs at most the one in-flight message.

- **No `commit_on`** → fire-and-forget: the cursor advances whether or not downstream
  nodes succeed.
- **`commit_on: "<node id>"`** → the cursor only advances past a message once that
  node's step is `Succeeded` (a not-taken `condition` counts as committed too). Point
  it at your `write_email` node so a message is never dropped just because a *later*
  enrichment step failed.

## 5. Idempotent redelivery

On a re-run of an already-stored message, `write_email` reports
`newly_written: false`. That **latches the run as a redelivery**: the executor
auto-**skips** every non-idempotent downstream node (an `llm_agent`, `label_email`,
`notify`, `webhook`, `create_note`…) so you don't double-classify or double-notify,
while the keyed write still runs to advance the cursor. Need a node to run anyway? Set
its `rerun_on_redelivery: true`.

## 6. Run it now

`POST /automations/{name}/collect` polls immediately instead of waiting for the next
`every` bucket — handy for testing. The first poll processes ≤200 messages,
steady-state ≤1000 per poll.

**Next:** enrich each stored message with labels — see the `email-tagging` article.

title: Tag email with an LLM classifier
summary: Extend email ingestion with an LLM step that reads each message and applies free-text labels (receipt, newsletter, urgent) via the label_email action.
body_md:
# Tag email with an LLM classifier

Build on `email-ingestion`: after each message is stored, have an LLM read it and set
free-text **labels** on the stored email. The `label_email` action records a
classifier verdict as a **full replace** of the email's label set. (Labels live on
catalerum's own `Email.labels` field — catalerum never writes them back to
Gmail/JMAP.)

## The graph

`collect_email → write_email → llm_agent (classify) → label_email`

```json
{ "graph": {
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "collect", "kind": "trigger", "trigger": {
        "kind": "collect_email", "connection": "<connection-id>",
        "every": "5m", "commit_on": "store"
    }, "position": { "x": 0, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "store", "kind": "action", "action": { "kind": "write_email" },
      "position": { "x": 220, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "classify", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "llm_agent",
        "system": "Classify this email. Return JSON {\"labels\": [...]}, choosing zero or more of: receipt, newsletter, personal, work, urgent, spam.",
        "output": "json"
    }, "position": { "x": 440, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "tag", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "label_email",
        "labels": "{{ inputs.classify.labels }}"
    }, "position": { "x": 660, "y": 0 } }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "collect", "to": "store" },
    { "from": "store", "to": "classify" },
    { "from": "classify", "to": "tag" }
  ]
}}
```

## Why the order is fixed

`label_email` labels a message an upstream `write_email` **already stored** — it
resolves the target by `(mailbox, uid)` from the collected item. If the email isn't
stored yet the step fails (*"write it first with write_email"*). So `write_email` must
run before `label_email` in the same run.

## label_email params

- **`labels`** (required, string array) — the labels to set. A **full replace**, not
  an append, so pass the complete set each run. Templatable from an upstream node's
  output — here `{{ inputs.classify.labels }}` pulls the JSON array the `llm_agent`
  returned. Entries are trimmed and de-duplicated; an empty result fails the step.
- **`rerun_on_redelivery`** — by default `label_email` is skipped on a redelivered
  (already-seen) message; set `true` to re-label anyway.

## The classifier step

The `llm_agent` action with `output: "json"` returns structured output the
`label_email` node reads by name (`inputs.classify.labels`). Keep the `system` prompt
tight and give it a **closed label vocabulary** so the output stays consistent. For a
high-volume inbox, pin a cheaper `model` and a lower `reasoning_effort` on the action.

## Committing

Point `commit_on` at the **`store`** (`write_email`) node, not the classifier. A
message is then committed — and never re-ingested — as soon as it's durably stored; if
the LLM step has a bad day the message stays put and the classifier just runs again on
the next poll (it's non-idempotent, so on a redelivery it re-runs only when you set
`rerun_on_redelivery: true`).

title: Webhooks: inbound triggers and outbound calls
summary: Fire an automation from an external HTTP POST via the webhook trigger, and push data to other systems with the webhook action / send_webhook tool.
body_md:
# Webhooks: inbound triggers and outbound calls

Two independent building blocks share the "webhook" name: the **`webhook` trigger**
fires an automation when something POSTs to catalerum, and the **`webhook` action**
POSTs from catalerum to some other system.

## Inbound: the webhook trigger

Give the trigger a `path`; an authenticated `POST /webhooks/{path}` then fires every
enabled automation whose trigger matches that path exactly.

```json
{ "graph": {
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "hook", "kind": "trigger", "trigger": {
        "kind": "webhook", "path": "/deploy-done"
    }, "position": { "x": 0, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "note", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "create_note", "title": "Deploy finished"
    }, "position": { "x": 240, "y": 0 } }
  ],
  "edges": [ { "from": "hook", "to": "note" } ]
}}
```

Call it:

```
POST /webhooks/deploy-done
Authorization: Bearer <token with automation:write>
```

Details:

- The endpoint is **workspace-scoped and authenticated**, gated on `automation:write`.
  The path is normalized to exactly one leading slash and no trailing slash, so
  `/webhooks/deploy-done` matches trigger `path: "/deploy-done"`. Inner slashes are
  preserved (`/webhooks/ci/main/passed`).
- The response is `202 Accepted` with `{ "matched": N, "jobs": [ … ] }` — one durable
  job per matching automation.
- The request **body is accepted but currently ignored** — the trigger carries only
  the path. If you need the caller to pass a JSON payload *today*, use a **named
  signal** (below).

### Need a payload, or a public (no-login) URL?

The named-signal surface is the sibling of webhooks and does carry a body:

- `POST /triggers/{name}` (authenticated) fires the `trigger` node kind (a named
  signal) and forwards the JSON body as `payload` your nodes can read.
- `POST /triggers/mint/{name}` mints a signed, short-lived **public** link; an external
  caller redeems it at `POST /triggers/fire/{token}` with no login (the HMAC token *is*
  the capability). Use this for third parties you can't hand a workspace token.

## Outbound: the webhook action

The **`webhook` action** (backed by the `send_webhook` tool, gated `web:write`) POSTs
to an external URL. Every field is templatable, so you can forward upstream results.

```json
{ "id": "notify", "kind": "action", "action": {
    "kind": "webhook",
    "url": "https://hooks.example.com/catalerum",
    "method": "post",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <your-token>" },
    "payload": { "event": "summarized", "text": "{{ inputs.summarize.summary }}" }
}, "position": { "x": 480, "y": 0 } }
```

Params:

- **`url`** (required) — absolute `http(s)`. Guarded by an SSRF policy (URL +
  DNS-rebind checks) before delivery.
- **`payload`** — JSON body, sent as `application/json`. Mutually exclusive with
  `body`; if both are omitted it sends `{}`.
- **`body`** + **`content_type`** — raw string body for non-JSON receivers
  (`content_type` defaults to `text/plain`).
- **`headers`** — extra request headers. Transport/hop-by-hop headers (`Host`,
  `Content-Length`, `Content-Type`, …) are refused.
- **`method`** — `post` (default), `put`, or `patch`.
- **`timeout_secs`** — capped at 300.

A non-2xx response from the receiver **fails the step**; redirects are not followed.
The action is non-idempotent, so on a collect redelivery it's auto-skipped (see
`email-ingestion`).

## End-to-end: relay a deploy notice

`POST /webhooks/deploy-done` → `summarize` the payload → `webhook` action to your
chat's incoming-webhook URL. Inbound fires it; outbound fans it out.

title: Index a GitHub wiki with embeddings and serve it over MCP
summary: Clone a GitHub wiki in a terminal, land each page in storage, embed-index it on every file event, then expose a prefix-scoped semantic-search MCP endpoint scoped to that wiki.
body_md:
# Index a GitHub wiki with embeddings and serve it over MCP

This recipe turns a GitHub wiki (or any git repo of Markdown) into a **prefix-scoped
semantic-search MCP endpoint** — an AI assistant can then answer questions grounded in
that wiki, and *only* that wiki. Four stages: clone → land files → embed-index → serve.

Requires an execution backend (`[exec]`, for the terminal) and a vector backend
(`[qdrant].enabled`, for indexing/search).

## Stage 1 — Clone the wiki and land it in storage

A GitHub wiki is a git repo (`https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.wiki.git`). Clone it in an
ephemeral terminal, then `persist_terminal` snapshots the working directory into object
storage under a `prefix` — writing each file as its own object.

```json
{ "graph": {
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "sched", "kind": "trigger", "trigger": {
        "kind": "schedule", "cron": "0 3 * * *"
    }, "position": { "x": 0, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "open", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "open_terminal", "backend": "sandbox"
    }, "position": { "x": 200, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "clone", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "terminal_write",
        "session_id": "{{ inputs.open.session_id }}",
        "data": "git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/acme/handbook.wiki.git wiki\n"
    }, "position": { "x": 400, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "land", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "persist_terminal",
        "session_id": "{{ inputs.open.session_id }}",
        "prefix": "wiki/",
        "source_subdir": "wiki"
    }, "position": { "x": 600, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "shut", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "close_terminal",
        "session_id": "{{ inputs.open.session_id }}"
    }, "position": { "x": 800, "y": 0 } }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "sched", "to": "open" },
    { "from": "open", "to": "clone" },
    { "from": "clone", "to": "land" },
    { "from": "land", "to": "shut" }
  ]
}}
```

- **`open_terminal`** `backend`: `local` | `sandbox` | `container` | `kubernetes`; its
  output carries a `session_id` every later terminal node chains off
  (`{{ inputs.open.session_id }}`).
- **`persist_terminal`** — `prefix` (required, the object-key prefix everything lands
  under, e.g. `wiki/`) and `source_subdir` (copy only the cloned `wiki` folder, not the
  whole workdir). Each landed file emits a per-file storage event.

Run this on a `schedule` to keep the mirror fresh — a re-clone re-lands changed pages,
which re-fires the indexer below.

## Stage 2 — Index each file on its storage event

Landing files fires a **`storage_object`** trigger per file. A second automation
listens for those events and (re)indexes the page, using a `condition` node to route
index-vs-delete on the event.

```json
{ "graph": {
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "evt", "kind": "trigger", "trigger": {
        "kind": "storage_object",
        "event": "created", "bucket": "docs", "prefix": "wiki/",
        "extensions": ["md", "markdown"]
    }, "position": { "x": 0, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "route", "kind": "condition",
      "runtime": "js",
      "source": "return trigger.event !== 'deleted';",
      "position": { "x": 220, "y": 0 } },
    { "id": "index", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "index_document",
        "bucket": "{{ trigger.bucket }}",
        "key": "{{ trigger.key }}",
        "operation": "index"
    }, "position": { "x": 440, "y": -60 } },
    { "id": "deindex", "kind": "action", "action": {
        "kind": "index_document",
        "bucket": "{{ trigger.bucket }}",
        "key": "{{ trigger.key }}",
        "operation": "delete"
    }, "position": { "x": 440, "y": 80 } }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "evt", "to": "route" },
    { "from": "route", "to": "index",   "from_port": "true" },
    { "from": "route", "to": "deindex", "from_port": "false" }
  ]
}}
```

- The **`storage_object`** trigger matches on `event` (`created` | `updated` |
  `deleted`), `bucket` (set it to the store your terminal snapshot lands in), optional
  `prefix`, and an optional `extensions` allow-list.
- A **`condition`** node routes execution down its `"true"` / `"false"` out-edge ports
  (set each edge's `from_port`). Here a non-delete event goes to `index`, a delete to
  `deindex`.
- **`index_document`** embeds and upserts one object (`operation: "index"`) or removes
  it (`operation: "delete"`), keyed by `bucket` + `key` templated from the trigger.
  It's idempotent.
- To backfill the whole wiki at once (e.g. right after the first clone), use
  **`reindex_objects`** with `key_prefix: "wiki/"` instead of waiting for per-file
  events (`limit` 1–5000, default 500).

## Stage 3 — Serve it as a scoped MCP endpoint

Indexed chunks are searchable with the `search_semantic` tool, narrowable by
`key_prefix` — that prefix scoping is the whole trick. Qdrant has no prefix operator,
so each vector denormalizes every directory-boundary ancestor of its key into an array
(`wiki/handbook/onboarding.md` → `["wiki/", "wiki/handbook/"]`); a subdir search is
then an exact array match.

Create an **MCP endpoint** — a small stored JavaScript program that declares one MCP
tool and calls `search_semantic` — pinned to this wiki's `bucket_name` + `key_prefix`:

```
POST /mcp-endpoints
{
  "name": "acme-handbook",
  "description": "Search the Acme company handbook.",
  "bucket_name": "docs",
  "key_prefix": "wiki/",
  "enabled": true,
  "script": "if (input.method === 'tools/list') { return [{ name: 'search_handbook', description: 'Search the Acme handbook', inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: { query: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['query'] } }]; } if (input.method === 'tools/call') { return catalerum.callTool('search_semantic', { query: input.arguments.query }); }"
}
```

The endpoint runs on its **own isolated tool registry** — the *only* host tool its
script can reach is `search_semantic`, and the host **force-injects** the endpoint's
`bucket_name` + `key_prefix` on top of whatever the script passes. A script can never
widen its own reach: even if it asks for `key_prefix: "other/"`, it still only searches
`wiki/`. That guarantee is enforced at the host bridge *and* the Qdrant filter, not by
capabilities.

Serve it two ways:

- **`POST /mcp/e/acme-handbook`** — under a workspace bearer token; the caller's
  workspace decides which endpoints are reachable.
- **`POST /mcp/s/{token}`** — **public, no login.** Mint the token with
  `POST /mcp-endpoints/{id}/token` (`ttl_days`, default 90, range 1–365); it returns
  `{ token, path, expires_at }`. The signed token carries `{ workspace, endpoint,
  expiry }`; anything bad, expired, or disabled is an opaque 404. Hand this URL to an
  external assistant to give it read-only, wiki-scoped RAG.

## Putting it together

Stage 1 (scheduled clone) keeps the mirror fresh → Stage 2 (per-file events) keeps the
index in sync → Stage 3 (scoped endpoint) serves it. Point an MCP-speaking assistant at
`/mcp/s/{token}` and it can answer from the handbook and nothing else.
